Harbor Town Reopens Its Century-Old Ferry Line

By Staff Reporter

The small ferry that once carried mail, cattle and schoolchildren across the bay made its first passenger crossing in eleven years on Saturday morning, after a long campaign by residents who argued that the boat was the only practical link between the two halves of the county. Dozens of people lined the pier before sunrise to watch it leave.

The vessel, a squat green boat with a wheelhouse barely large enough for two people, was restored over three winters by a group of retired shipwrights who met every Tuesday in a borrowed shed near the old cannery. They replaced most of the hull planking, rebuilt the engine from salvaged parts and repainted the name on the bow by hand.

County officials had closed the route after a storm damaged the landing on the northern shore and an inspection found the boat unfit for service. Repairing both was estimated at the time to cost more than the ferry earned in a decade, and the council voted to replace it with a bus that takes a forty minute detour around the head of the bay.

Residents of the northern villages said the bus never worked for them. Fishermen could not carry their gear on it, older people found the long ride exhausting, and the timetable was cut twice as passenger numbers fell. A petition to restore the ferry gathered more signatures than there are registered voters in the three northern parishes combined.

The restoration was paid for by a mixture of small donations, a grant from a maritime heritage fund and the proceeds of a summer fair that has become a local fixture. The landing was rebuilt by volunteers using timber donated by a sawmill upriver, with a structural engineer from the regional authority checking the work at each stage.

Under the new arrangement the ferry will run four times a day during the summer and twice a day in winter, weather permitting. Fares will be kept low, and children travelling to the secondary school on the southern shore will ride free. The operators say they expect the service to cover its running costs within two years.

Not everyone is convinced. One councillor who voted against the original closure warned that a single breakdown could leave the northern villages without a crossing for weeks, and urged the county to keep the bus route in reserve. The operators replied that a second engine has already been sourced and stored, and that the bus will continue on a reduced schedule.

For many of the people on the pier, the arguments mattered less than the sight of the boat pulling away from the shore. An elderly woman who said she had crossed on the ferry every week as a girl stood at the rail with her granddaughter, pointing out the lighthouse, the seal rocks and the chapel on the hill as they passed.

The operators plan to hold an open day next month, when visitors will be able to tour the wheelhouse and the engine room and hear from the volunteers who restored the vessel. A small exhibition of photographs from the ferry's early years will be displayed in the waiting room on the southern landing for the rest of the season.
